questions.question: Define biodegradable, explain why most plastics are not biodegradable, and state the three conditions that make a biodegradable claim meaningful.
questions.expected_answer: Biodegradable means able to be broken down by living organisms, mainly bacteria and fungi, into simple natural substances: water, carbon dioxide, minerals and compost. Most plastics (polythene, polystyrene, PVC) are long carbon chains that no organism can digest, so they persist for centuries, breaking only into microplastic fragments in sunlight. A meaningful claim must state the time (months, not decades), the conditions (home compost heap or only an industrial composter) and the residue (harmless compost, not toxic fragments or microplastics). Compostable is the stricter term: breaks down in a compost heap within a set time leaving safe compost.

questions.question: Describe the four life-cycle stages used to judge whether a material is environmentally friendly, with an example of a good choice at each stage.
questions.expected_answer: Source: renewable or recycled rather than non-renewable, for example bagasse from sugar-cane waste, plantation timber, recycled PET. Manufacture: low energy, water and pollution, for example recycled paper or recycled aluminium (about five percent of the energy of new), sun-dried earth blocks instead of fired brick. Use: durable and reused many times, for example a cotton bag used hundreds of times or a refillable glass bottle. Disposal: can be composted or recycled rather than landfilled, for example paper, bagasse and untreated wood composted, aluminium and PET recycled, in a circular approach where one product's end is another's start.

questions.question: Compare polystyrene and bagasse takeaway boxes across the life cycle, state the verdict, and explain why a paper bag versus a polythene bag comparison is less clear.
questions.expected_answer: Source: polystyrene from non-renewable oil; bagasse from renewable sugar-cane waste. Manufacture: polystyrene needs refining and chemical processing; bagasse is pulped, moulded and dried with modest energy. Use: both serve one meal, polystyrene insulating slightly better. Disposal: polystyrene never biodegrades and fragments into the environment; bagasse composts in months. Bagasse wins three stages and draws one, so it is the environmentally sound choice though it costs more. Paper versus polythene is less clear because paper is renewable and compostable but needs more energy and water to make and more fuel to transport, while polythene is light and cheap but persists for centuries; used once paper usually wins, but if the polythene bag is reused many times the balance shifts, so the assumptions about use must be stated.
